A photon. The fundamental quantum of electromagnetic radiation, the smallest indivisible unit of light and all forms of electromagnetic energy. It is a massless boson that mediates the electromagnetic force within the Standard Model. Photons carry energy proportional to their frequency via Planck's relation E equals h nu, where h is Planck's constant and nu is frequency. They travel at the speed of light in vacuum and embody the wave-particle duality central to quantum mechanics, behaving as waves exhibiting diffraction and interference, and as particles carrying discrete energy and momentum.

A photon has zero rest mass but carries energy E equals h nu and momentum p equals E divided by c equals h nu divided by c, where c is the speed of light. Photons are spin-one particles, massless vector bosons. The two spin states correspond to the two polarizations of light, vertical and horizontal, or left and right circular. In the quantum field picture, photons are excitations of the electromagnetic field. The number of photons in a region of space can fluctuate; even empty vacuum fluctuates with virtual photon pairs.

Photons do not decay. Once emitted, a photon can travel indefinitely or until absorbed by matter. An electron absorbing a photon gains its energy; an electron dropping to a lower energy state emits a photon. The photoelectric effect, discovered by Einstein in nineteen oh-five, demonstrated that photons are quantized: a single photon must have enough energy to eject an electron from a metal surface, no matter how intense the light. This disproved the classical wave picture. High-energy photons like X-rays and gamma rays can create particle-antiparticle pairs in the presence of a nucleus. Low-energy photons like radio and microwave waves are absorbed and re-emitted as thermal radiation. Photons are the gauge bosons of electromagnetism in the Standard Model and exemplify the dual nature of quantum objects.
